One of the most common concerns people have after suffering an injury in a car accident, truck collision, or workplace incident is whether they can afford to hire a lawyer. The contingency fee system removes that barrier entirely. Under this arrangement, your attorney does not charge any fees upfront — instead, the lawyer's payment comes as a percentage of the compensation recovered in your case. If your case does not result in a settlement or verdict, you owe nothing for legal representation. The Legal Information Institute at Cornell Law School provides a helpful overview of how contingency fees operate in the American legal system.

What Is a Contingency Fee?

A contingency fee is a payment arrangement between a client and an attorney in which the attorney's fee is contingent upon — that is, depends on — winning the case. Unlike hourly billing or flat-fee arrangements common in other areas of law, the contingency fee model means:

  • No retainer — you do not pay a lump sum upfront to hire the attorney
  • No hourly billing — the attorney does not track hours and bill you monthly
  • Payment only from recovery — the attorney receives a pre-agreed percentage of the settlement or verdict
  • No recovery, no fee — if the case is unsuccessful, the attorney earns nothing for their time and effort

This system exists specifically to ensure that injury victims have access to legal representation regardless of their financial situation. Whether you are facing mounting medical bills from a motorcycle accident or have lost income due to a workplace injury, the contingency fee model means you can pursue justice without taking on additional financial risk.

How the Contingency Fee System Works

The contingency fee process follows a clear sequence:

Step 1: Free Initial Consultation

Most personal injury attorneys offer a free case evaluation where they review the facts of your accident, assess the strength of your claim, and explain your legal options. If the attorney believes you have a viable case, they will offer to represent you under a contingency fee agreement.

Step 2: Signing the Contingency Fee Agreement

This written contract spells out the exact terms — including the fee percentage, how expenses are handled, and what happens if the case is unsuccessful. In both Georgia and South Carolina, this agreement must be in writing; South Carolina also requires the client to sign it.

Step 3: The Attorney Handles Your Case

Your attorney investigates the accident, gathers evidence, negotiates with insurance companies, and — if necessary — files a lawsuit and takes the case to trial. Throughout this process, you pay nothing out of pocket for the attorney's time.

Step 4: Settlement or Verdict

If the case results in a settlement or jury verdict, the attorney's fee is calculated as a percentage of the total recovery. The fee, along with any case expenses, is deducted from the settlement before the remaining funds are distributed to you.

Step 5: If the Case Is Unsuccessful

If no compensation is recovered, you owe the attorney nothing for their legal services. The attorney absorbs the cost of the time invested in your case; whether you owe advanced expenses depends on the agreement — at Roden Law, there are no fees or costs with no recovery.

What "No Upfront Costs" Really Means

When a personal injury law firm advertises "no upfront costs," this typically means two things:

No attorney fees upfront: You do not pay for the lawyer's time until and unless the case is won. This is the core contingency fee promise.

The firm advances case expenses: Personal injury cases involve costs beyond attorney time — filing fees, medical record retrieval, expert witness fees, court reporter fees, accident reconstruction costs, and more. Under most contingency fee arrangements, the law firm advances these expenses and recoups them from the settlement or verdict. If the case is unsuccessful, many firms absorb these costs entirely, though this varies by firm and should be clarified in your fee agreement.

This is why it is essential to read your contingency fee agreement carefully and ask questions about expense handling before signing.

Typical Contingency Fee Percentages

Contingency fees in personal injury cases are commonly one-third (33.3%) of the recovery, often higher if a lawsuit is filed or the case is tried:

Stage of CaseCommon FeeExplanation
Pre-litigation settlement33.3% (one-third)Case settles before a lawsuit is filed
Post-filing / pre-trial33.3% – 40%Lawsuit is filed; case settles during litigation
Trial or appealOften 40%Case requires full trial preparation and/or courtroom presentation

Workers' compensation fees follow separate rules: in Georgia they need State Board of Workers' Compensation approval and are capped at 25% (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-108), and in South Carolina they are up to 33.3% with Commission approval (S.C. Code Regs. 67-1205).

The fee percentage often increases as the case progresses because the attorney's investment of time, resources, and risk increases at each stage. A case that settles quickly requires fewer resources than one that goes through discovery, depositions, expert testimony, and a multi-day trial.

Case Expenses vs. Attorney Fees

It is important to understand the difference between attorney fees and case expenses:

Attorney fees are the percentage of the recovery that compensates the lawyer for their legal work — strategy, negotiation, legal research, court appearances, and client communication.

Case expenses (also called "costs" or "disbursements") are the out-of-pocket costs associated with building and prosecuting the case:

  • Court filing fees — required to initiate a lawsuit
  • Medical record retrieval — fees charged by hospitals and doctors to copy medical files
  • Expert witness fees — payments to medical experts, accident reconstructionists, economists, and vocational specialists
  • Deposition costs — court reporter fees for recording sworn testimony
  • Process server fees — costs of formally delivering legal documents to defendants
  • Investigation costs — hiring investigators, obtaining police reports, and gathering surveillance footage
  • Postage and copying — administrative costs throughout the case

Most personal injury firms advance these costs and deduct them from the settlement. Whether expenses are deducted before or after the attorney fee is calculated can significantly affect your net recovery — always clarify this in your fee agreement.

Contingency Fee Rules in Georgia and South Carolina

Georgia Rules

Georgia's Rules of Professional Conduct (Georgia Rule 1.5) govern contingency fee arrangements. Key requirements include:

  • Written agreement required: All contingency fee agreements must be in writing and state the percentage(s) for settlement, trial or appeal (Rule 1.5(c)(1))
  • Fee must be reasonable: The fee percentage must be reasonable in light of the complexity, risk, and amount of work involved
  • Prohibited cases: Contingency fees are not permitted in criminal defense cases, or in domestic relations matters when the fee depends on securing a divorce or on the amount of alimony, support or a property settlement
  • Expense disclosure: The agreement must state the litigation and other expenses to be deducted from the recovery and whether they are deducted before or after the fee is calculated
  • Statute of limitations: Georgia's 2-year statute of limitations for personal injury claims (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) makes it important to consult an attorney promptly — delaying can forfeit your right to file
  • Comparative fault: Under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault, and you cannot recover if you are 50% or more at fault

South Carolina Rules

South Carolina's Rules of Professional Conduct (Rule 1.5) impose similar requirements with some differences:

  • Written agreement required: Must be signed by the client and state the percentage(s) for settlement, trial or appeal, the expenses to be deducted, whether they come off before or after the fee, and any expenses the client will be expected to pay
  • Reasonableness standard: South Carolina courts apply a reasonableness test considering the complexity, amount involved, and customary fees in the locality
  • Prohibited cases: Same restrictions on criminal and most domestic relations cases
  • Client's right to terminate: A client can terminate the contingency fee arrangement at any time, though the attorney may be entitled to compensation for work already performed (quantum meruit)
  • Statute of limitations: South Carolina's 3-year statute of limitations (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) provides more time but should not encourage delay
  • Comparative fault: South Carolina bars recovery only if you are 51% or more at fault — slightly more favorable than Georgia's threshold

Advantages of the Contingency Fee System

The contingency fee model offers significant advantages for accident victims:

Access to Justice

Most accident victims cannot afford to pay a lawyer by the hour — often hundreds of dollars an hour — while simultaneously dealing with medical bills, lost wages, and recovery. The contingency fee system ensures that financial resources do not determine who can obtain quality legal representation. Whether your claim involves a slip and fall, medical malpractice, or a wrongful death, the contingency fee system levels the playing field.

Aligned Incentives

Because the attorney only gets paid when you get paid, their financial interests are directly aligned with yours. Your attorney is motivated to maximize your recovery because their fee is a percentage of that recovery. This creates a partnership where both you and your lawyer benefit from the best possible outcome.

Risk Transfer

The attorney assumes the financial risk of the case. For example, if a case takes two years and $50,000 in expenses but ultimately fails, a firm that does not charge costs on a loss — as Roden Law does not — absorbs that loss, not you. This risk-sharing arrangement gives injury victims the ability to pursue legitimate claims without fear of financial ruin.

Quality Screening

Because attorneys bear the risk of losing their investment, they are selective about which cases they accept on contingency. If an experienced personal injury attorney agrees to take your case, it is a strong signal that they believe your claim has merit. This screening function benefits both clients and the legal system.

Questions to Ask Before Signing a Contingency Fee Agreement

Before entering a contingency fee arrangement, ask your attorney these important questions:

  1. What is the fee percentage, and does it change if the case goes to trial? Understand the fee structure at every stage of the case.
  2. Are case expenses deducted before or after the attorney fee? This affects how much you ultimately receive.
  3. What happens to expenses if the case is unsuccessful? Some firms absorb costs; others require reimbursement.
  4. Are there any costs I might be responsible for regardless of outcome? Clarify any exceptions to the "no fee unless we win" promise.
  5. How will I receive updates on my case and expenses? Establish expectations for communication and financial transparency.
  6. Can I terminate the agreement, and what are the consequences? Understand your right to change attorneys if needed.
  7. Will the settlement check come through a trust account? Ethical rules require attorneys to hold settlement funds in a client trust account and provide a detailed disbursement statement.

How Roden Law's Contingency Fee Model Works

At Roden Law, we believe that every accident victim in Georgia and South Carolina deserves access to experienced legal representation regardless of their financial situation. Our contingency fee model is designed with your interests in mind:

  • Free consultation: Your case evaluation costs nothing. We will review the facts, assess your claim, and give you honest advice about your options.
  • No upfront costs: You pay nothing to hire us. We typically advance the costs of your case — filing fees, expert witnesses, medical records, and investigation costs.
  • You pay only if we recover: Our fee comes exclusively from the compensation we recover for you. Fees and costs apply only upon successful recovery — if there is no recovery, you owe no fees and no costs.
  • Transparent agreements: We explain every term of our fee agreement in plain language before you sign, and we welcome questions at every stage of the process.

Our firm handles cases across every major practice area — from brain injuries and spinal cord injuries to premises liability and pedestrian accidents. No matter the complexity of your case, our contingency fee model ensures that cost is never a barrier to pursuing justice.

If you or a loved one has been injured due to someone else's negligence, contact Roden Law today for a free, no-obligation consultation. Call 1-844-RESULTS — there is no risk and no cost to learn about your legal options.

After an accident caused by someone else's negligence, one of the most important decisions you will make is whether to hire a personal injury lawyer. Studies consistently show that injury victims who are represented by an attorney recover significantly more compensation than those who handle claims on their own. According to the Cornell Law Institute's overview of personal injury law, injured parties have the legal right to seek damages for both economic losses and the intangible impact an injury has on their quality of life — but exercising that right effectively requires understanding the law, the evidence needed, and the tactics insurance companies use to minimize payouts.

At Roden Law, our attorneys have recovered over $300 million for injury victims across Georgia and South Carolina. We have seen firsthand how legal representation changes outcomes — and how costly it can be for accident victims to navigate the claims process alone.

Why You Need a Personal Injury Lawyer After an Accident

The days and weeks following an accident are overwhelming. You are dealing with pain, medical appointments, missed work, and mounting bills — all while an insurance company is pressuring you to accept a quick settlement. A personal injury lawyer steps in to handle the legal and financial complexity of your claim so you can focus on recovery.

The core benefits of hiring an attorney include:

  • Protecting you from costly mistakes — giving a recorded statement, signing a medical authorization, or accepting an early settlement can permanently damage your claim. An attorney ensures you do not unknowingly waive your rights.
  • Leveling the playing field — insurance companies have teams of adjusters, investigators, and defense attorneys working to minimize your payout. Your attorney is the counterweight to that entire operation.
  • Maximizing your compensation — experienced attorneys know how to calculate the full value of a claim, including future damages that most accident victims overlook.
  • Meeting critical deadlines — personal injury claims in Georgia and South Carolina are subject to strict filing deadlines. Missing a deadline means losing your right to compensation entirely.
  • Taking your case to trial if necessary — insurance companies are far more likely to offer fair settlements when they know your attorney is prepared to litigate.

How Insurance Companies Work Against You

Insurance companies are businesses, and their profitability depends on paying out as little as possible on claims. When you file a car accident claim or any other personal injury claim without an attorney, you are negotiating against professionals whose entire job is to reduce your settlement.

Common insurance company tactics include:

Requesting a Recorded Statement Early

An adjuster may call within days of your accident and ask you to provide a recorded statement about what happened. This is not a neutral fact-finding exercise. The adjuster is looking for inconsistencies, admissions of fault, or statements that can be used to argue your injuries are less serious than claimed. A personal injury attorney will advise you on what to say — or handle all communication with the insurer directly.

Offering a Quick, Low Settlement

Insurance companies frequently make settlement offers within the first few weeks after an accident, before you fully understand the extent of your injuries. These offers rarely account for future medical treatment, long-term pain and suffering, or reduced earning capacity. Once you accept a settlement, you sign a release that prevents you from pursuing additional compensation — even if your condition worsens.

Disputing the Severity of Your Injuries

Insurers may argue that your injuries are pre-existing, unrelated to the accident, or not as serious as your medical records indicate. They may request access to your entire medical history looking for prior conditions they can use to reduce your claim. An attorney limits the scope of medical releases and counters these arguments with expert medical evidence.

Delaying the Claims Process

Some insurance companies deliberately drag out the process, hoping financial pressure will force you to accept a lower offer. When you have an attorney, the insurer knows that unnecessary delay could result in a lawsuit — which is more expensive for them than settling fairly.

Accurately Calculating the Full Value of Your Claim

One of the most significant advantages of hiring a personal injury lawyer is getting an accurate assessment of what your claim is actually worth. Most accident victims dramatically underestimate the value of their case because they only consider the bills they have received so far.

An experienced attorney calculates your damages across every category, including:

Economic Damages

  • Medical expenses — emergency treatment, hospital stays, surgery, diagnostic imaging, physical therapy, chiropractic care, prescription medications, and medical equipment
  • Future medical costs — projected expenses for ongoing treatment, rehabilitation, pain management, or future surgeries related to your injury
  • Lost wages — income you missed during recovery, including salary, hourly wages, bonuses, commissions, and benefits
  • Reduced earning capacity — if your injury limits your ability to perform your job or advance in your career, the difference in lifetime earning potential is a compensable loss
  • Property damage — vehicle repair or replacement costs and other personal property destroyed in the accident
  • Out-of-pocket expenses — transportation to medical appointments, home modifications, household help, and other costs directly caused by the injury

Non-Economic Damages

  • Pain and suffering — the physical pain you have endured and will continue to endure as a result of the injury
  • Emotional distress — anxiety, depression, PTSD, insomnia, and other psychological effects of the accident and injury
  • Loss of enjoyment of life — the inability to participate in activities, hobbies, and experiences you enjoyed before the injury
  • Loss of consortium — the impact the injury has had on your relationship with your spouse or family members
  • Scarring and disfigurement — the physical and emotional toll of visible injuries that permanently alter your appearance

In cases involving grossly negligent or reckless behavior — such as drunk driving or extreme speeding — you may also be able to pursue punitive damages designed to punish the at-fault party.

Building a Strong Case With Evidence and Experts

Proving that another party's negligence caused your injury — and that your damages are as significant as you claim — requires substantial evidence. An experienced personal injury attorney knows exactly what evidence is needed and how to obtain it.

Your attorney's investigation typically includes:

  • Accident scene evidence — photographs, video footage, skid marks, road conditions, traffic signals, and any physical evidence from the scene
  • Police and incident reports — official documentation of the accident, including any citations issued to the at-fault party
  • Witness statements — testimony from people who saw the accident occur or arrived at the scene immediately after
  • Medical records and expert opinions — your complete treatment history, along with testimony from medical professionals about the nature, severity, and long-term prognosis of your injury
  • Accident reconstruction — in complex cases such as truck accidents or multi-vehicle collisions, your attorney may retain accident reconstruction experts to demonstrate exactly how the crash occurred and who was at fault
  • Economic analysis — forensic economists or vocational rehabilitation experts can calculate the financial impact of your injury on your current and future earning capacity
  • Electronic evidence — cell phone records, vehicle black box data, dashcam footage, and surveillance video that may support your version of events

Without an attorney, most accident victims simply do not have the knowledge, resources, or access to gather this level of evidence. And without strong evidence, the insurance company has the upper hand in negotiations.

State Laws That Affect Your Claim in Georgia and South Carolina

Personal injury law varies significantly from state to state. If your accident occurred in Georgia or South Carolina, several state-specific rules directly impact your right to recover compensation and the amount you may receive.

Statute of Limitations

Every personal injury claim must be filed within a strict deadline. If you miss this deadline, you permanently lose your right to sue — no matter how strong your case is.

State Filing Deadline Statute
Georgia 2 years from the date of injury O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33
South Carolina 3 years from the date of injury S.C. Code § 15-3-530

An attorney ensures your claim is filed well within these deadlines and that all necessary paperwork, evidence, and documentation are prepared properly. Cases involving government entities may have even shorter notice requirements, making early legal consultation critical.

Comparative Fault Rules

Both Georgia and South Carolina follow modified comparative fault systems, meaning your compensation can be reduced — or eliminated — if you are found partially at fault for the accident.

Rule Georgia South Carolina
Standard Modified comparative fault Modified comparative fault
Threshold Recovery barred if 50% or more at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) Recovery barred if 51% or more at fault
Effect Damages reduced by your percentage of fault Damages reduced by your percentage of fault
Example 30% at fault on $100,000 claim = $70,000 recovery 30% at fault on $100,000 claim = $70,000 recovery

Insurance companies routinely try to assign a higher percentage of fault to the injured party to reduce their payout. An attorney fights back against inflated fault allocations by presenting evidence that accurately establishes liability. This is especially important in cases like motorcycle accidents and pedestrian accidents, where bias against the injured party is common.

Common Personal Injury Cases That Benefit From Legal Representation

While every accident case benefits from having an attorney, certain types of personal injury claims are particularly complex and difficult to navigate without legal representation. Roden Law handles cases across Georgia and South Carolina including:

  • Car accidents — from rear-end collisions to multi-vehicle pileups, car accident claims involve insurance disputes, liability questions, and often significant injuries requiring long-term treatment
  • Truck accidents — commercial truck crashes involve federal regulations, multiple liable parties (driver, trucking company, cargo loader), and catastrophic injuries that demand substantial compensation
  • Motorcycle accidents — riders face bias from insurers and juries, and the severity of motorcycle injuries makes accurate damage calculation critical
  • Slip and fall accidents — premises liability claims require proving that the property owner knew about or should have known about the hazardous condition
  • Medical malpractice — these cases require expert medical testimony and navigating complex procedural requirements specific to each state
  • Wrongful death — when an accident results in a fatality, surviving family members face both devastating grief and complicated legal proceedings to recover damages
  • Brain injuries — traumatic brain injuries often have long-term or permanent effects that require lifetime care, making future damage calculation essential
  • Spinal cord injuries — the catastrophic nature of spinal injuries means the stakes in these claims are exceptionally high
  • Workers' compensation claims — workplace injuries involve a separate legal system with its own rules, deadlines, and benefit calculations

Regardless of the type of accident, having a qualified attorney ensures that every aspect of your claim is handled properly and that no category of damages is overlooked.

What to Look for When Hiring a Personal Injury Attorney

Not all personal injury lawyers offer the same level of experience, resources, or commitment to their clients. When evaluating attorneys, consider these important factors:

Experience With Your Type of Case

Personal injury law covers a wide range of accidents and injuries. Look for an attorney or firm with specific experience handling cases similar to yours. A firm that has handled thousands of car accident and personal injury claims will have a deeper understanding of the evidence, experts, and strategies needed to maximize your recovery.

Trial Experience

Most personal injury cases settle before trial, but the insurance company's willingness to offer a fair settlement depends heavily on whether your attorney is prepared to go to court. Attorneys who never try cases have less leverage in negotiations. Choose a firm with a proven track record of both successful settlements and trial verdicts.

Resources to Investigate and Build Your Case

Complex personal injury claims require resources — accident reconstruction experts, medical specialists, forensic economists, and the staff to manage extensive documentation. A well-resourced firm can invest in your case without cutting corners.

Clear Communication

Your attorney should keep you informed about the progress of your case, explain legal concepts in plain language, and be responsive when you have questions. You are trusting this person with one of the most important legal matters of your life — communication matters.

A Track Record of Results

Ask about the firm's case results, including settlement amounts and verdict amounts for cases similar to yours. At Roden Law, we have recovered over $300 million for clients across more than 5,000 cases — results that reflect our commitment to maximizing compensation for every client.

How Contingency Fee Arrangements Work

Many accident victims hesitate to hire an attorney because they worry about the cost — especially when they are already facing medical bills and lost income. The contingency fee model eliminates that barrier entirely.

Under a contingency fee arrangement:

  • You pay nothing upfront — there are no retainer fees, hourly billing, or out-of-pocket costs to get started
  • Your attorney typically advances case costs — investigation expenses, expert witness fees, filing fees, and other costs are covered by the firm during the case
  • You only pay if you win — the attorney's fee is a percentage of the compensation recovered on your behalf. If the case is unsuccessful, you owe nothing
  • Your interests are aligned — because the attorney only gets paid from the recovery, they are financially motivated to maximize the value of your claim

This arrangement means that anyone can access experienced legal representation after an accident, regardless of their financial situation. It also means there is zero financial risk to you for consulting with an attorney about your case.

Talk to an Attorney About Your Case Today

If you were injured in an accident caused by someone else's negligence in Georgia or South Carolina, hiring an experienced personal injury lawyer is the single most important step you can take to protect your rights and maximize your compensation. The insurance company has a team working to minimize your payout — you deserve someone fighting just as hard on your side.

Roden Law offers free, confidential case reviews with no obligation. Our attorneys serve clients from six offices across Georgia and South Carolina, and we handle every case on a contingency fee basis — you pay nothing unless we win.

Do not let the insurance company decide what your claim is worth. The experienced personal injury attorneys at Roden Law will evaluate your case, explain your options, and fight for every dollar of compensation you are owed.

When a car crash, truck collision, or motorcycle wreck leads to serious injuries, the question of how the accident happened often becomes the centerpiece of your legal claim. An accident reconstructionist uses scientific methods, engineering principles, and advanced technology to recreate the crash scene and establish fault. For injury victims in Georgia and South Carolina, having an expert reconstructionist can mean the difference between a denied claim and a substantial recovery. Roden Law works with leading accident reconstruction professionals to build the strongest possible cases for our clients across both states. For a deeper understanding of how accident reconstruction experts work, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) provides detailed resources on crash investigation methodology.

What Is an Accident Reconstructionist?

An accident reconstructionist is a specially trained expert who investigates crash scenes using physics, engineering, and forensic analysis to determine how and why an accident occurred. These professionals typically hold degrees in mechanical engineering, physics, or forensic science, and many have backgrounds in law enforcement crash investigation units. Reconstructionists differ from general witnesses because they apply the scientific method to physical evidence. Rather than offering subjective opinions, they use measurable data — skid mark lengths, crush depths, vehicle rest positions, and road geometry — to develop mathematically supported conclusions about vehicle speeds, impact angles, and driver behavior before the crash. Both sides in a personal injury case may retain their own reconstructionist. The plaintiff's expert may demonstrate that the defendant was speeding or distracted, while the defense expert may attempt to shift blame to the injured party. This is particularly important in states like Georgia and South Carolina, where comparative fault rules can reduce or eliminate your recovery based on your percentage of responsibility.

How Accident Reconstruction Works

The reconstruction process follows a systematic approach that typically unfolds in several phases:

Scene Documentation and Evidence Collection

The reconstructionist begins by visiting the crash site — sometimes within hours of the accident, other times weeks or months later. They document road conditions, traffic control devices, sight lines, grade and curvature of the road, and any physical evidence remaining at the scene such as gouge marks, fluid stains, or debris fields.

Vehicle Inspection

Each vehicle involved undergoes detailed inspection. The expert measures crush damage using industry-standard protocols, examines tire conditions, checks brake and steering components for pre-crash defects, and downloads data from the vehicle's Event Data Recorder (EDR) — sometimes called the car's "black box." EDR data can reveal pre-impact speed, brake application timing, throttle position, and seatbelt usage in the seconds before the crash.

Physics-Based Analysis

Using the collected evidence, the reconstructionist applies principles of Newtonian physics — conservation of energy, conservation of momentum, and friction dynamics — to calculate vehicle speeds at impact, the point of impact within the roadway, and the sequence of events leading to the collision.

Computer Simulation and Animation

Modern reconstructionists often use specialized software to create computer simulations and 3D animations of the crash. These visual tools make complex physics concepts accessible to jurors and insurance adjusters, illustrating exactly how the collision unfolded from multiple perspectives.

Types of Evidence Reconstructionists Analyze

A thorough reconstruction examines multiple categories of evidence to piece together the complete picture:
Evidence Type What It Reveals
Skid marks and tire marks Pre-crash braking, speed, and vehicle path
Vehicle crush damage Impact speed and direction of force (Delta-V)
Event Data Recorder (EDR) Speed, braking, throttle, seatbelt use in final seconds
Road surface and geometry Contributing factors like poor drainage, sight obstructions
Traffic camera and dashcam footage Real-time visual record of the crash sequence
Witness statements Corroborate or challenge physical evidence findings
Medical records Injury patterns consistent with reconstructed impact forces
Weather and lighting data Visibility conditions at the time of the crash
The reconstructionist synthesizes all of these data points into a cohesive narrative that can withstand cross-examination in court. This multi-source approach is especially valuable in truck accident cases, where electronic logging device (ELD) data, driver qualification files, and vehicle maintenance records add additional layers of evidence to analyze.

When Your Case Needs an Accident Reconstructionist

Not every car accident claim requires expert reconstruction. For minor fender-benders with clear liability, police reports and photographs may be sufficient. However, several scenarios make reconstruction analysis essential:
  • Disputed liability — When both drivers blame each other, objective scientific analysis can establish who truly caused the crash
  • No independent witnesses — Without eyewitness testimony, physical evidence becomes the primary means of proving fault
  • Serious or fatal injuries — High-stakes cases with significant damages justify the investment in expert analysis and often require it to overcome aggressive defense tactics
  • Hit-and-run accidents — Reconstructionists can sometimes identify the type of vehicle involved and its travel direction from physical evidence left at the scene
  • Complex multi-vehicle crashes — When three or more vehicles are involved, determining the initial point of impact and chain reaction requires expert analysis
  • Suspected mechanical defect — If brake failure, tire blowout, or steering malfunction may have caused the crash, reconstruction can identify product liability issues
  • Contradicted police reports — Officers arrive after the fact and sometimes reach incorrect conclusions about fault

Accident Reconstruction in Georgia and South Carolina

The legal frameworks in Georgia and South Carolina create specific contexts where reconstruction evidence becomes particularly valuable.

Georgia Expert Witness Standards

Georgia follows a modified version of the Daubert standard for admitting expert testimony under O.C.G.A. § 24-7-702. To be admissible, the reconstructionist's testimony must be based on sufficient facts, be the product of reliable principles and methods, and reflect a reliable application of those principles to the case facts. Georgia's modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) means a plaintiff recovers nothing if found 50% or more at fault — making accurate fault determination through reconstruction critical to case outcomes. Georgia's two-year statute of limitations for personal injury (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) means evidence preservation must begin immediately. Physical evidence at the crash scene degrades quickly, and vehicles may be repaired or scrapped, making early engagement of a reconstructionist essential.

South Carolina Expert Witness Standards

South Carolina applies Rule 702, SCRE, which similarly requires that expert testimony be based on reliable methodology. South Carolina's modified comparative fault system allows recovery as long as the plaintiff is less than 51% at fault. With a three-year statute of limitations (S.C. Code § 15-3-530), there is slightly more time to gather evidence, but physical evidence still deteriorates, and the sooner a reconstructionist is retained, the more reliable the analysis will be.

Types of Accidents That Benefit From Reconstruction

Accident reconstruction proves valuable across many case types that Roden Law handles throughout Georgia and South Carolina:
  • Car accidents — Intersection collisions, head-on crashes, and rear-end impacts with disputed speeds
  • Truck accidents — Commercial vehicle crashes involving driver fatigue, improper loading, or equipment failure, where federal motor carrier regulations add complexity
  • Motorcycle accidents — Visibility disputes and left-turn crashes where the at-fault driver claims they never saw the rider
  • Pedestrian accidents — Speed analysis and reaction time calculations to determine whether the driver could have stopped
  • Bicycle accidents — Establishing right-of-way violations and unsafe passing distances
  • Wrongful death cases — Fatal crashes where the victim cannot testify, making physical evidence paramount
  • Boating accidents — Marine collision reconstruction using water current, wake patterns, and navigational data

How Reconstructionist Testimony Strengthens Your Claim

Expert reconstruction testimony impacts your case at multiple stages of the claims process:

During Insurance Negotiations

A detailed reconstruction report signals to the insurance company that your claim is supported by scientific evidence, not just your word against the other driver's. Adjusters know that juries find expert testimony persuasive, which motivates more reasonable settlement offers. Many cases settle after the insurer reviews the reconstruction report without ever going to trial.

At Depositions and Mediation

The reconstructionist's analysis provides concrete talking points during depositions and mediation sessions. When opposing counsel or a mediator asks how you know the other driver was speeding, the answer is backed by measurable data — crush depth calculations, EDR readouts, and momentum analysis — rather than subjective testimony.

At Trial

If your case goes to trial, the reconstructionist testifies as a qualified expert witness. They present their methodology, findings, and conclusions to the jury, often using 3D animations and visual aids. Jurors consistently rate expert reconstruction testimony among the most influential evidence in determining fault in motor vehicle cases.

How a Personal Injury Attorney Works With Reconstructionists

Hiring an accident reconstructionist on your own can cost thousands of dollars. When you retain a personal injury attorney at Roden Law, the firm covers all upfront costs of expert retention — including reconstruction fees — as part of our contingency fee arrangement. You pay nothing unless we win compensation for you. Your attorney coordinates the entire process: identifying the right expert for your case type, ensuring evidence is preserved before it disappears, directing the scope of the investigation, and preparing the reconstructionist for deposition and trial testimony. This collaboration between legal strategy and scientific analysis builds the most compelling case possible. If you were injured in a crash in Georgia or South Carolina and fault is in dispute, contact Roden Law for a free consultation. Our attorneys will evaluate whether accident reconstruction analysis could strengthen your claim and connect you with the right experts. Call 1-844-RESULTS or contact us online today.

Table of Contents

  • Common Types of Medical Malpractice

When you visit a doctor, hospital, or other healthcare provider, you trust that the care you receive will meet basic professional standards. But when a medical professional's negligence causes injury or worsens your condition, you may have a medical malpractice case. Understanding whether your experience qualifies as malpractice—rather than simply an unfortunate medical outcome—is the first critical step toward holding negligent providers accountable. Both Georgia and South Carolina law provide legal remedies for patients harmed by substandard medical care, though each state has distinct procedural requirements and deadlines that can significantly impact your case.

What Is Medical Malpractice?

Medical malpractice occurs when a healthcare provider deviates from the accepted standard of care in their medical community, and that deviation directly causes injury to a patient. The "standard of care" refers to what a reasonably competent healthcare professional with similar training and experience would have done under the same or similar circumstances. It is important to understand that not every bad medical outcome qualifies as malpractice. Medicine involves inherent risks, and even the best doctors cannot guarantee positive results. The key distinction is whether the healthcare provider acted negligently—meaning they failed to exercise the degree of care, skill, and treatment that a reasonable provider would have used in the same situation. Medical malpractice can be committed by any licensed healthcare professional, including physicians, surgeons, nurses, anesthesiologists, pharmacists, dentists, chiropractors, and other specialists. Hospitals and medical facilities can also be held liable for systemic failures, staffing issues, or the actions of their employees.

Four Elements of a Medical Malpractice Claim

To successfully pursue a medical malpractice case in either Georgia or South Carolina, you must establish four essential elements. Failing to prove any one of these elements will likely result in an unsuccessful claim.

1. Duty of Care

You must show that a doctor-patient relationship existed, meaning the healthcare provider owed you a duty of care. This relationship is typically established when a provider agrees to treat you, examines you, or provides a diagnosis. Emergency room visits, scheduled appointments, and surgical consultations all create this duty.

2. Breach of the Standard of Care

You must demonstrate that the provider failed to meet the accepted standard of care. This requires showing what a competent provider would have done and how the defendant's actions fell short. Expert medical testimony is almost always required to establish this element in both Georgia and South Carolina.

3. Causation

You must prove that the provider's breach of duty directly caused your injury. This means the harm you suffered would not have occurred "but for" the provider's negligence. In cases involving wrongful death, causation must link the negligent medical care to the patient's death.

4. Damages

You must show that you suffered actual, compensable damages as a result of the malpractice. This includes medical bills, lost wages, pain and suffering, and other losses directly tied to the injury caused by the negligent care.

Common Types of Medical Malpractice

Medical malpractice takes many forms. Some of the most common types of cases our attorneys handle include:
Type of Malpractice Description Examples
Misdiagnosis or Delayed Diagnosis Failing to correctly identify a condition or taking too long to diagnose it Cancer misdiagnosed as a benign condition; heart attack symptoms dismissed as anxiety
Surgical Errors Mistakes made during surgery Wrong-site surgery, leaving instruments inside a patient, nerve damage from improper technique
Medication Errors Prescribing or administering the wrong medication or dosage Dangerous drug interactions, overdoses, allergic reactions from unreviewed patient history
Birth Injuries Harm to mother or baby during labor and delivery Cerebral palsy from oxygen deprivation, brachial plexus injuries, failure to perform emergency C-section
Anesthesia Errors Mistakes in administering or monitoring anesthesia Incorrect dosage, failure to review medical history, inadequate monitoring during surgery
Failure to Treat Correctly diagnosing a condition but failing to provide appropriate treatment Premature discharge, failure to refer to a specialist, ignoring test results
These cases frequently overlap with other personal injury claims. For example, a surgical error during treatment for a traumatic brain injury or spinal cord injury could give rise to both the original injury claim and a separate medical malpractice claim against the treating facility.

Signs You May Have a Medical Malpractice Case

Determining whether you have a viable malpractice case can be challenging without legal and medical expertise. However, several warning signs suggest you should consult an attorney:
  • Your condition worsened after treatment — If you were getting better and then deteriorated after a procedure, medication change, or hospital stay, something may have gone wrong.
  • Your symptoms were dismissed or ignored — If you repeatedly reported symptoms that were not taken seriously, leading to a delayed diagnosis, this may constitute negligence.
  • You developed a new condition after treatment — Infections acquired in the hospital, nerve damage from surgery, or organ damage from medication errors are all potential malpractice indicators.
  • A different doctor expressed concern — If a second-opinion physician questioned the treatment you received or indicated it was below standard, this is a significant red flag.
  • Your recovery timeline is far longer than expected — While some variation is normal, dramatically extended recovery may indicate complications caused by negligent care.
  • You were not informed of risks — Under the informed consent doctrine, providers must explain the risks, benefits, and alternatives of a procedure before performing it. Failure to obtain proper consent can itself be malpractice.
  • A loved one died unexpectedly during routine care — Unexpected death during routine or low-risk procedures warrants immediate investigation into whether malpractice occurred.

Medical Malpractice Laws: Georgia vs. South Carolina

While both states allow patients to sue for medical malpractice, there are critical differences in how each state handles these claims.

Georgia Medical Malpractice Law

Statute of Limitations: Under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71, you generally have two years from the date of the negligent act to file a medical malpractice lawsuit in Georgia. However, there is a statute of repose of five years, meaning no case can be brought more than five years after the negligent act, regardless of when the injury was discovered. For minors under age five, the deadline extends until the child's seventh birthday. Expert Affidavit Requirement: Georgia law (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-9.1) requires that a medical malpractice complaint be accompanied by an expert affidavit from a qualified medical professional. This affidavit must state that at least one act of negligence occurred and identify the specific negligent act. Failure to include this affidavit will result in dismissal of the case. Comparative Fault: Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33. You can recover damages as long as you are less than 50% at fault, but your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault. Damage Caps: Georgia previously had caps on noneconomic damages in medical malpractice cases, but the Georgia Supreme Court struck down these caps as unconstitutional in Atlanta Oculoplastic Surgery v. Nestlehutt (2010). Currently, there are no caps on damages in Georgia medical malpractice cases.

South Carolina Medical Malpractice Law

Statute of Limitations: Under S.C. Code § 15-3-545, you have three years from the date of the treatment or the date the injury was discovered (or should have been discovered) to file a medical malpractice lawsuit. South Carolina also imposes a six-year statute of repose from the date of the alleged negligent act. For minors, the deadline is extended during minority, but by no more than seven years and no more than one year after the child turns eighteen (S.C. Code § 15-3-545(D)). Notice of Intent Requirement: South Carolina law requires that you file a Notice of Intent to File Suit, together with an expert affidavit specifying at least one negligent act or omission, and serve it on each defendant before filing the lawsuit (S.C. Code §§ 15-79-125, 15-36-100). Filing the notice tolls (pauses) the statute of limitations, and the parties must then mediate, generally within 90 to 120 days of service, before the lawsuit can be filed. Comparative Fault: South Carolina uses a modified comparative negligence system. You can recover damages if your fault is less than 51%, with your award reduced proportionally. Damage Caps: Under S.C. Code § 15-32-220, South Carolina caps noneconomic damages in medical malpractice cases at a base of $350,000 per provider or institution and $1,050,000 in total per claimant, adjusted each year for inflation ($596,001 and $1,788,002 for 2026).
Factor Georgia South Carolina
Filing Deadline 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71) 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-545)
Statute of Repose 5 years 6 years
Expert Affidavit Required at filing Required with Notice of Intent
Pre-Suit Notice Not required Notice of Intent with expert affidavit, then mediation
Damage Caps None (struck down 2010) $596,001 per provider / $1,788,002 total (2026; adjusted yearly)
Comparative Fault Modified — under 50% Modified — under 51%

How to Prove a Medical Malpractice Case

Medical malpractice cases require extensive evidence and expert testimony. Building a strong case involves several critical steps: Obtain Complete Medical Records: Your attorney will request all medical records related to the treatment in question, including physician notes, nursing logs, medication administration records, imaging studies, lab results, and surgical reports. Both Georgia and South Carolina law entitle patients to copies of their medical records. Retain Qualified Expert Witnesses: Expert testimony is essential in virtually every medical malpractice case. The expert must practice in the same or similar specialty as the defendant and can explain how the standard of care was breached. In Georgia, the expert must be competent to testify about the specific procedures at issue. In South Carolina, the expert must be licensed and either board certified in the relevant specialty or have practiced or taught in it for at least three of the last five years immediately preceding the opinion (S.C. Code § 15-36-100). Document Your Damages: Keep thorough records of all medical expenses, lost wages, rehabilitation costs, and how the injury has affected your daily life. Photograph visible injuries and maintain a journal documenting your pain levels, limitations, and emotional distress. Establish the Timeline: Medical malpractice cases often hinge on timing—when symptoms appeared, when diagnoses were made, and when treatment was administered or delayed. A clear timeline helps demonstrate how the negligent act caused your injury. These evidentiary requirements are similar to those in other complex injury cases, such as product liability claims or nursing home abuse cases, where expert testimony and detailed documentation are essential to proving liability.

Damages You Can Recover

If you can prove that medical malpractice caused your injury, you may be entitled to compensation for:
  • Medical expenses — Past and future costs of treatment related to the malpractice injury, including surgery, medication, rehabilitation, and ongoing care
  • Lost wages — Income lost during recovery and reduced future earning capacity if the injury prevents you from returning to your previous occupation
  • Pain and suffering — Physical pain, emotional distress, anxiety, depression, and loss of enjoyment of life caused by the injury
  • Loss of consortium — Compensation for the impact on your relationship with your spouse
  • Disfigurement or disability — Compensation for permanent physical changes or functional limitations resulting from the negligent care
  • Wrongful death damages — If a loved one died due to malpractice, surviving family members may pursue a wrongful death claim for funeral expenses, lost financial support, and loss of companionship
In Georgia, there are currently no caps on any category of damages in medical malpractice cases. In South Carolina, noneconomic damages are subject to the caps described above under S.C. Code § 15-32-220, but economic damages (medical bills, lost wages) are not capped.

Common Defenses in Medical Malpractice Cases

Healthcare providers and their insurance companies use several strategies to fight malpractice claims:
  • The treatment met the standard of care — The defendant will retain their own expert witnesses to testify that the care provided was reasonable and appropriate.
  • The injury was pre-existing or unrelated — Defendants may argue that your condition was caused by something other than their treatment, similar to defenses raised in car accident cases involving pre-existing injuries.
  • Contributory negligence — The provider may claim you contributed to your own injury by failing to follow medical advice, missing follow-up appointments, or not disclosing important medical history.
  • Informed consent — If you signed a consent form acknowledging the risks of a procedure, the defendant may argue you accepted those risks. However, consent forms do not protect providers who perform procedures negligently.
  • Statute of limitations — If you file outside the applicable deadline, the defendant will seek dismissal regardless of the merits of your case.

How a Medical Malpractice Lawyer Can Help

Medical malpractice cases are among the most complex areas of personal injury law. They require specialized medical knowledge, extensive expert networks, and significant financial resources to litigate effectively. An experienced medical malpractice attorney can:
  • Evaluate your case with qualified medical experts to determine if malpractice occurred
  • Handle the expert affidavit requirement in Georgia or the Notice of Intent process in South Carolina
  • Obtain and analyze complex medical records to identify deviations from the standard of care
  • Calculate the full value of your damages, including future medical needs and lost earning capacity
  • Negotiate with hospital insurance companies and defense counsel who handle these cases regularly
  • Take your case to trial if a fair settlement cannot be reached
At Roden Law, our attorneys handle medical malpractice cases across Georgia and South Carolina on a contingency fee basis—you pay nothing unless we recover compensation for you. If you believe you or a loved one was harmed by negligent medical care, contact us today for a free consultation or call 1-844-RESULTS. Time limits apply to every medical malpractice claim, so do not wait to explore your legal options.

  • Talk to an Experienced Medical Malpractice Lawyer

When you seek medical care, you trust that the professionals treating you will act competently and in your best interest. Unfortunately, that trust is sometimes broken. Medical errors are one of the leading causes of death and serious injury in the United States, and patients in Georgia and South Carolina are not immune. If you or a loved one has been harmed by a healthcare provider's negligence, understanding how medical malpractice law works is the first step toward holding the responsible parties accountable and recovering the compensation you deserve.

This guide explains what medical malpractice is, the types of cases we see most often, how these claims work in both Georgia and South Carolina, and what to expect from the legal process.

What Is Medical Malpractice?

Medical malpractice occurs when a healthcare provider — a doctor, surgeon, nurse, hospital, pharmacist, or other medical professional — causes harm to a patient by failing to provide care that meets the accepted standard in their field. It is not simply a bad outcome; medicine involves inherent risks, and not every complication or unsuccessful treatment constitutes malpractice.

For an injury to qualify as medical malpractice, three conditions must be present:

  1. The provider deviated from the standard of care — they did something a reasonably competent provider in the same specialty would not have done, or failed to do something they should have done
  2. The deviation caused the patient harm — there must be a direct link between the provider's error and the injury
  3. The patient suffered measurable damages — medical expenses, lost income, pain and suffering, or other compensable losses

A poor bedside manner, a long wait time, or a treatment that simply did not work as hoped are not malpractice. But a surgeon who operates on the wrong limb, a doctor who misreads a scan and misses cancer, or a pharmacy that dispenses a lethal drug combination — those are clear examples of providers falling below the standard of care.

The Standard of Care: The Legal Benchmark

The "standard of care" is the central concept in every medical malpractice case. It is defined as the level and type of care that a reasonably competent healthcare provider in the same specialty would provide under similar circumstances. This standard is not perfection — it is reasonable competence.

The standard is established through expert testimony. In both Georgia and South Carolina, a medical malpractice case cannot proceed without a qualified expert — a licensed physician or specialist in the same field as the defendant — who testifies about what the standard of care required and how the defendant fell short.

Important nuances:

  • The standard varies by specialty — what is expected of a general practitioner differs from what is expected of a neurosurgeon
  • The standard accounts for the information available at the time — a doctor is not judged by information discovered after the fact
  • Local practice patterns may be considered, but the standard is generally national in scope for specialists
  • Emergency situations may alter what constitutes reasonable care, given the time pressure and limited information available

Common Types of Medical Malpractice

Medical malpractice takes many forms. The most common types of cases our attorneys handle across Georgia and South Carolina include:

Misdiagnosis and Delayed Diagnosis

When a doctor fails to diagnose a condition — or diagnoses it too late for effective treatment — the consequences can be devastating. Cancer that could have been treated at an early stage becomes terminal. A heart attack dismissed as indigestion leads to permanent cardiac damage. A stroke mistaken for a migraine results in brain injury. Diagnostic errors are the most common type of medical malpractice claim in the United States.

Surgical Errors

Surgical mistakes include operating on the wrong body part, damaging adjacent organs or nerves during a procedure, leaving surgical instruments or sponges inside the body, and performing unnecessary surgery. These "never events" — so named because they should never happen — represent some of the clearest cases of malpractice.

Medication Errors

Prescribing the wrong medication, the wrong dosage, or a drug that interacts dangerously with the patient's other medications. Pharmacy dispensing errors — giving the wrong pills or mislabeling a prescription — also fall into this category. Medication errors can cause organ damage, allergic reactions, overdoses, or death.

Birth Injuries

Negligent obstetric care during pregnancy, labor, or delivery can cause catastrophic injuries to both mother and child. Common birth injuries include cerebral palsy, Erb's palsy (brachial plexus injury), brain damage from oxygen deprivation, and maternal hemorrhage. These cases often involve the failure to perform a timely C-section, improper use of forceps or vacuum extractors, or failure to monitor fetal distress.

Anesthesia Errors

Too much anesthesia can cause brain damage or death. Too little can result in the patient waking during surgery — a terrifying experience called anesthesia awareness. Anesthesiologists can also be liable for failing to review the patient's medical history for contraindications, intubation injuries, or inadequate post-operative monitoring.

Emergency Room Negligence

Emergency rooms operate under extreme time pressure, but that does not excuse negligence. Common ER malpractice includes premature discharge of patients with serious conditions, failure to order appropriate diagnostic tests, misreading X-rays or CT scans, and failure to consult specialists when the patient's condition warrants it.

Nursing Home Neglect and Abuse

Nursing home neglect — including inadequate staffing, failure to prevent falls, medication mismanagement, bedsore development, and malnutrition — is a growing area of medical malpractice law. When facilities fail to provide adequate care, residents suffer preventable injuries and illness.

Who Can Be Held Liable?

Medical malpractice liability can extend well beyond the individual doctor who made the error. Multiple parties can be responsible:

  • Individual physicians, surgeons, and specialists — for errors in diagnosis, treatment, or surgical technique
  • Hospitals and medical facilities — for institutional negligence such as inadequate staffing, poor training, equipment failures, and negligent credentialing of physicians
  • Nurses, physician assistants, and other staff — for medication administration errors, monitoring failures, or failure to communicate critical information
  • Pharmacies — for dispensing errors
  • Nursing homes and long-term care facilities — for neglect and abuse
  • Medical device and pharmaceutical manufacturers — when a defective medical device or drug contributes to the injury

Identifying all liable parties is critical because it directly affects the total compensation available — particularly in South Carolina, where the non-economic damage cap applies per provider or institution, up to a total per claimant (S.C. Code § 15-32-220).

What You Need to Prove a Medical Malpractice Case

A successful medical malpractice claim requires proving four elements by a preponderance of the evidence:

  1. Provider-patient relationship (Duty) — The healthcare provider owed you a duty of care. This is established by showing a treatment relationship existed.
  2. Breach of the standard of care — The provider failed to act as a competent provider in the same specialty would have under similar circumstances. This must be established through expert testimony.
  3. Causation — The provider's breach directly caused your injury. The defense will argue your injury was caused by your underlying condition, not the provider's error — so expert testimony linking the breach to the harm is essential.
  4. Damages — You suffered compensable harm: medical expenses, lost income, pain and suffering, or other losses.

The expert testimony requirement is what makes medical malpractice cases fundamentally different from other personal injury claims like car accidents or slip and falls. Without a qualified expert willing to testify that the standard of care was breached, the case cannot proceed.

Georgia vs. South Carolina: Key Legal Differences

While the basic elements of a malpractice claim are the same in both states, the procedural rules and damage limits differ significantly:

Rule Georgia South Carolina
Statute of limitations 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71) 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-545)
Statute of repose 5 years 6 years
Non-economic damage cap None (struck down in 2010) $596,001 per provider / $1,788,002 total (2026; adjusted yearly)
Punitive damage cap $250K (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1) 3x compensatory or $739,245 (2026; adjusted yearly)
Pre-suit requirement Expert affidavit at filing (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-9.1) Notice of Intent filed with expert affidavit (S.C. Code §§ 15-79-125, 15-36-100)
Mandatory mediation No Yes

For detailed breakdowns of each state's rules, see our state-specific guides: Medical Malpractice Limits in Georgia and Medical Malpractice Limits in South Carolina.

Types of Compensation Available

Medical malpractice victims may recover several categories of damages:

Economic Damages (No Cap in Either State)

  • Medical expenses — corrective surgeries, hospitalization, rehabilitation, medication, medical devices, and projected future medical costs
  • Lost wages — income lost during recovery and treatment
  • Lost earning capacity — permanent reduction in your ability to earn a living
  • Out-of-pocket costs — transportation to medical appointments, home modifications, in-home care

Non-Economic Damages

  • Pain and suffering — physical pain caused by the malpractice and subsequent corrective treatments
  • Emotional distress — anxiety, depression, PTSD, loss of trust in medical providers
  • Loss of enjoyment of life — inability to participate in activities, relationships, and daily functions
  • Loss of consortium — impact on your spousal relationship
  • Disfigurement — permanent scarring or physical changes from the medical error

Non-economic damages are uncapped in Georgia but subject to South Carolina's cap of $596,001 per provider or institution and $1,788,002 in total for 2026 (S.C. Code § 15-32-220).

Punitive Damages

Available only in cases of egregious, willful, or reckless conduct. Punitive damages are capped at $250,000 in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1) and at three times compensatory damages or $739,245, the 2026 inflation-indexed figure, in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-32-530), whichever is greater.

Wrongful Death

When medical malpractice causes a patient's death, surviving family members may file a wrongful death claim to recover compensation for their losses. In Georgia, the limitation period runs from the date of death. In South Carolina, a malpractice death claim is subject to the medical-malpractice limitations provisions, including S.C. Code § 15-3-545: the deadline can depend on when the treatment occurred and when the claim was or reasonably should have been discovered, a six-year repose period generally applies, and the wrongful death period does not revive a malpractice claim that was already barred before the death.

The Medical Malpractice Case Process: Step by Step

Medical malpractice cases follow a more complex process than typical personal injury claims. Here is what to expect:

1. Initial Consultation and Case Evaluation

Your attorney reviews the basic facts, obtains your medical records, and makes a preliminary assessment of whether the case has merit. This stage is free at Roden Law.

2. Medical Record Review and Expert Consultation

Your attorney retains a qualified medical expert in the relevant specialty to review all records and determine whether the standard of care was breached. This is the most critical step — without a supportive expert opinion, the case cannot proceed.

3. Pre-Suit Requirements

In Georgia, your attorney prepares the expert affidavit required at the time of filing (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-9.1). In South Carolina, your attorney files a Notice of Intent to File Suit together with a qualified expert's affidavit, and serves it on all defendants; filing it tolls the statute of limitations (S.C. Code §§ 15-79-125, 15-36-100).

4. Filing the Lawsuit

The complaint is filed in the appropriate court, identifying the defendants, describing the negligence, and specifying the damages sought.

5. Discovery

Both sides exchange evidence — medical records, expert reports, depositions of the treating physicians and the plaintiff, and interrogatories. Discovery is often the longest phase of the case.

6. Mediation / Settlement Negotiations

Most malpractice cases settle before trial. In South Carolina, mediation is mandatory before the lawsuit is filed (S.C. Code § 15-79-125). Your attorney negotiates from a position of strength based on the expert evidence and the full documentation of your damages.

7. Trial (if Necessary)

If settlement negotiations fail, the case proceeds to a jury trial. Your attorney presents expert testimony, medical evidence, and damage documentation to the jury, which determines liability and the amount of compensation.

Why Medical Malpractice Cases Are Uniquely Difficult

These cases are among the most challenging in personal injury law. Several factors make them exceptionally complex:

  • Expert requirements — you cannot file or win without qualified medical experts willing to testify against fellow healthcare providers
  • High litigation costs — expert witness fees, medical record analysis, depositions, and trial preparation make these cases expensive
  • Aggressive defense — hospitals and their malpractice insurers employ well-funded legal teams and their own experts
  • Complex medical evidence — jurors must understand technical medical concepts to evaluate the claim
  • Strict procedural rules — pre-suit requirements, damage caps, and short deadlines create traps for the unprepared
  • Emotional difficulty — reliving a traumatic medical experience through depositions and testimony takes a personal toll

This is why choosing an attorney with specific experience in medical malpractice — not just personal injury generally — is so important. The stakes are too high and the process too specialized for a generalist approach.

Talk to an Experienced Medical Malpractice Lawyer

If you believe you or a loved one was harmed by medical negligence in Georgia or South Carolina, time is critical. Filing deadlines are strict, pre-suit requirements demand months of preparation, and evidence can be lost or altered the longer you wait.
